body.heading: No gaps, no overlaps
paragraphs: A tessellation covers a flat surface with shapes that meet perfectly — no gaps, no overlaps. If you insist on using just one regular shape (all sides and angles equal), only three can do it: the equilateral triangle, the square and the regular hexagon.

The reason is arithmetic wearing a disguise. At every corner where tiles meet, the angles must add to exactly 360 degrees. A triangle's corner is 60 degrees, and six of them make 360. A square's 90 fits four times. A hexagon's 120 fits three times. A pentagon's corner is 108 — and 360 refuses to divide by it. That is the whole secret.

body.heading: Bees knew first
paragraphs: Honeybees build their combs from hexagons, and the choice is elegant engineering: of the shapes that tile, the hexagon encloses the most area for the least wax. Evolution found the efficient answer long before mathematicians proved it — the honeycomb conjecture was only formally proved in 1999.

Humans tile for the same twin reasons: strength and beauty. Roman mosaics, Islamic geometric tilework and your bathroom floor are all answers to the same question — how do we cover this surface completely, and make it worth looking at?

body.heading: Try it: tile detectives and tile designers
paragraphs: Go on a tiling hunt at home: floors, brick walls (a staggered tessellation of rectangles), paving, quilts. Photograph each pattern and name the shape doing the work. Brickwork is the sneaky one — rectangles offset by half, so the corners still meet perfectly.

Then design your own: cut twenty identical shapes from card — try a kite or an arrowhead — and see whether they tile. When a shape refuses, ask what small notch or bump would fix it. You are one step from Escher's studio.

takeaway: Tessellation is arithmetic you can walk on: corners must sum to 360, and only three regular shapes in the world can manage it alone.
